title: The Czech Board narrows the next decision to a hold or a rise
summary: The CNB left the two-week repo rate at 3.75% by unanimous vote on September 17. Its guidance was unusually specific: the next meeting would consider keeping rates unchanged or raising them. The Bank judged June’s increase sufficient to tighten conditions so far and pointed to a separate rise in longer-term rates that should stabilize growth in new loans. At the same time, commodity-market developments had intensified upside risks. The current hold and the narrower set of future options should be represented as separate pieces of information in a historical policy series (September statement, decision).

The domestic economy had slowed without showing an equivalent disappearance of cost pressures. GDP growth eased from 2.2% to 1.9% year on year in the second quarter, with domestic demand still the main source of growth. Household consumption and business investment were rising. Unemployment was low. Wage growth showed no new acceleration but remained sufficiently rapid, in the Board’s assessment, to sustain pressure in services and property prices. A decline in the acceleration of wages is different from a decline in the wage-growth rate to a level consistent with target inflation and productivity growth (economic developments).

The longer end of the curve was doing part of the work of policy. Higher long rates raise the cost of fixed-term borrowing and can affect new mortgages or business financing before another change in the repo rate. The Board expected slower growth in new credit; it did not report a measured causal fall in loan volumes. Demand, lending standards, maturity preferences and government borrowing could alter the observed outcomes. Credit growth and debt financing of higher public expenditure continued to expand the quantity of money, which the Board saw as a reason to maintain restraint (decision and risks).

The new commodity risk worked through multiple routes. Energy and other input costs can affect current prices directly, but sustained effects on expectations and wage claims would matter more for monetary policy over its horizon. The Board expected a temporary increase in headline inflation around the turn of the year, with core inflation still elevated. It described the overall risk balance as inflationary, while retaining weak euro-area growth, possible global asset corrections and trade barriers as downside risks. This was an updated assessment of the summer outlook. The statement did not publish new annual point forecasts (decision and risks).

For event analysis, the most informative move could be at the next meeting horizon rather than in the already determined September rate. A comparison of forward rates immediately after the rate announcement with those after the 15:00 briefing can test whether the explicit hold-or-hike guidance changed market probabilities. Longer bond yields must also be interpreted relative to foreign yields, issuance and term premia. Their rise before this meeting was part of the Board’s reasoning, not evidence of a subsequent surprise generated by the statement (decision and publication schedule).

questions.question: How much did ruling the next decision down to two options change pricing?
questions.detail: Estimate the next-meeting rate implied before the decision, after the 14:30 rate announcement and after the press statement. Use bid–ask ranges and allow for risk premia. A shift after the statement would be consistent with guidance about November even though the September vote was unanimous.

questions.question: Were higher longer-term rates slowing the flow of new loans?
questions.detail: Match new fixed-rate borrowing to the relevant maturity of the yield or swap curve. Separate approval, signing and drawdown dates and adjust for refinancing. Compare borrowers whose loan terms reset promptly with those insulated by existing fixed contracts.

questions.question: Could commodity costs feed wage claims even without an acceleration in aggregate pay?
questions.detail: Examine contract-renewal periods, union wage demands and sector-specific compensation measures, distinguishing highly energy-exposed sectors from labour-intensive services. The mean wage can be stable if some sectors accelerate while others weaken. Compare expectations at multiple horizons with realized price-setting patterns.
